newsitem.title: CHINA: China military plants seek cooperation with coast.
newsitem.headline: China military plants seek cooperation with coast.

text.p: Many Chinese military enterprises that moved to remote hinterlands to escape possible attack in the 1960s are signing contracts to boost cooperation with booming coastal regions, state media said on Sunday.
The bid by China's military industry to branch beyond its confines in less-developed western regions came as senior military leader Liu Huaqing called for faster development of the defence industry.

"With new technological revolutions progressing rapidly around the world, China should focus on promoting further development of its defence industry to help maintain world peace and national security," the Xinhua news agency quoted Liu, vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, as saying.

The army should learn from the advanced technology and draw on the experience of other countries, said Liu, the only representative of the military on the seven-member standing committee of the Politburo.
"Only by doing so can our army shoulder the heavy task of defending socialist modernisation, accomplishing national reunification and maintaining world peace," he said.

About 80 of China's hundreds of military companies signed 75 contracts worth 759 million yuan ($91.45 million) with deveopment zones at last week's National Fair for Cooperation between Military Enteprises and Development Zones, the China Daily Business Weekly said.
Some enterprises had agreed to set up factories in the development zones to make products for civilian use, it said.
Others entered contracts to sell their patented technology or machinery to civilian enterprises in the development zones or to cooperate in trade, the newspaper said.

Military enterprises have the advantages of relatively advanced technology, better-educated personnnel and more fixed assets, while the zones have capital, infrastructure, access to information and a better location for business, it said.
Civilian products accounted for 80 percent of the total industrial output of China's military companies in 1995.

Chinese figures show the declared profit of the People's Liberation Army in 1993 was $1.0 billion on turnover of $6-9 billion, but military analysts believe its real profits were at least double that from an industry that has been transformed into an economic powerhouse in the last decade.
